source.title_on_document: Evaluating AI-assisted creative ideation: A crossover study in higher education

supplement.where: No supplementary material or online appendix is referred to in the complete document (pp. 1-17), which ends with References and includes no appendix. This does not establish whether a separate supplement exists. Outcome statistics are reported in Tables 4-7 and Sections 4.2-4.3 (pp. 8-11); prompt statistics are in Tables 8-9 (p. 12). Data availability states: Data will be made available on request (p. 15).
supplement.holds: No statistics are identified in the document as available only in supplementary material.

paper_design_summary: In one two-hour session, 51 third-year industrial design engineering students at UPC (Spain) were randomly divided into two groups for a two-task crossover: Group A (n = 24) generated ideas unaided in Task 1 (improving public transport) and with ChatGPT (GPT-3.5) in Task 2 (improving university spaces); Group B (n = 27) did the reverse. Each task asked for eight handwritten and drawn ideas in 30 minutes (728 ideas in total). The researchers scored fluency, flexibility, originality (unique ideas and solutions), novelty (count of ideas resembling existing products), text and image elaboration, thematic homogenisation (diversity indices, category size, unique contributions), and semantic divergence of LaBSE embeddings of the idea descriptions.

studies.label: Randomised crossover ideation experiment, ChatGPT-assisted vs unaided (public transport and university spaces tasks, one session)

assignment.what_was_assigned: Order of conditions: unaided first, then ChatGPT (GPT-3.5) (Group A, n = 24), or ChatGPT first, then unaided (Group B, n = 27). Task order was fixed for everyone (Task 1 public transport, Task 2 university spaces), so condition and task are crossed by group, and each student did one task in each condition.
assignment.quote: a randomised controlled crossover experiment was employed, in which participants were randomly assigned to one condition for the first task and then switched to the other condition for the second task.
assignment.locator: p. 4, Section 3.2.1; pp. 4-5 ('They were then randomly divided into two groups'); p. 5, Fig. 1; p. 7, Table 3 note (Group A n = 24; Group B n = 27)

arms.name: AI-assisted
arms.description: Computer lab with university-owned computers and internet access limited to ChatGPT (GPT-3.5). Group B in Task 1 (27 students, 195 ideas) and Group A in Task 2 (24 students, 173 ideas); 368 ideas in all. Every participant did one task in this condition.

arms.name: Unaided
arms.description: Classroom with no computer access and no permission to use external resources or electronic devices. Group A in Task 1 (24 students, 158 ideas) and Group B in Task 2 (27 students, 202 ideas); 360 ideas in all. Every participant did one task in this condition.

participants.exclusions: No exclusions or attrition reported. The 51 students were randomly divided into Group A (n = 24) and Group B (n = 27) (Fig. 1, p. 5); Tables 3 and 5 report N = 51 with these group sizes, and Table 4 reports n = 51 per condition (N = 102 person-condition observations). For the qualitative prompt analysis only, 49 of 51 ChatGPT conversations were retrieved (p. 10).
participants.who: Third-year students in the bachelor's degree in industrial design engineering and product development, Universitat Politècnica de Catalunya · BarcelonaTech (UPC).
participants.quote: The study involved 51 third-year students from the bachelor's degree in industrial design engineering and product development at the Universitat Politècnica de Catalunya · BarcelonaTech (UPC), Spain.
participants.locator: p. 4, Section 3.1; p. 5, Fig. 1; p. 8, Table 4 note; p. 9, Table 5 note

ai_tool.how_used: Free use of ChatGPT on lab computers during the 30-minute task. Ideas were written and drawn by hand on pre-printed templates, so AI text was not pasted into the deliverable (p. 13). In the 49 retrieved conversations, students averaged 6.96 prompts (Table 8), and generic requests for ideas were the most frequent code, nearly half of the 341 coded units (48.39 percent; Table 9, p. 12; p. 13).

task.description: Generate eight innovative ideas, each on a separate pre-printed sheet with space for a drawing and a description: Task 1, improving public transport; Task 2, improving university spaces. The paper says the two tasks were designed to be comparable in difficulty, scope, and relevance.
task.duration: 30 minutes per task, within a two-hour session

outcomes.name: Fluency (number of ideas generated per participant)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Total number of ideas generated (Table 2, p. 7). The task asked for eight ideas in 30 minutes (p. 5). Fluency was the one variable that clearly violated the ANOVA assumptions, and the paper says results involving it 'should be interpreted with caution' (p. 6). Tests: Wilcoxon signed-rank within person (Table 4) and Mann-Whitney U by task (Table 5).

outcomes.name: Individual-level semantic divergence (spread of each participant's own ideas, LaBSE)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Idea descriptions transcribed by OCR with Gemini, checked by hand, and embedded with LaBSE (p. 7). Methods: 'the average pairwise semantic divergence within each participant's set of ideas was computed per condition' and compared with a paired samples t-test (p. 7). Results describe it as 'the average semantic divergence from the centroid per participant' (p. 10) without saying which centroid. Coded flexibility because the Methods measure variety among one person's own ideas; the paper presents it as individual-level homogenisation. The reported df (364) does not match 51 participants.

contrasts.control_arm: Unaided (within person, both tasks pooled)
contrasts.reported: Unaided M = 0.28 (SD = 0.03) vs AI-assisted M = 0.29 (SD = 0.03); paired samples t(364) = 3.41, p = .001, d = 0.48, 95 % CI [0.01, 0.03]. Direction follows the printed means and Fig. 3(b) (higher divergence with AI); the text concludes that participants 'generated more semantically concentrated ideas when using AI'.

outcomes.name: Group-level semantic divergence (cosine distance of each idea to its condition's centroid, LaBSE)
outcomes.question: across_people
outcomes.measure_detail: Cosine distance between each idea's LaBSE embedding and the average embedding of its condition (AI-assisted vs unaided), compared with an independent samples t-test (p. 7). Higher divergence means less homogeneous. Text from the handwritten sheets was transcribed by OCR with Gemini and checked by hand (p. 7).

contrasts.treatment_arm: AI-assisted ideas (368 ideas, both tasks pooled)
contrasts.control_arm: Unaided ideas (360 ideas, both tasks pooled)
contrasts.reported: Divergence to centroid: unaided M = 0.28 (SD = 0.06) vs AI-assisted M = 0.29 (SD = 0.07); independent samples t(728) = -3.54, p < .001, d = -0.26, 95 % CI [-0.03, -0.01]. Direction follows the printed means and Fig. 3(a) (higher divergence, so more spread, with AI); the text reads the result as AI-assisted ideas being 'modestly more semantically similar to the group centroid'.
contrasts.locator: p. 10, Section 4.3; p. 11, Fig. 3(a); idea counts p. 10 (N = 368, N = 360) and p. 5, Fig. 1

diversity_detail.metric: Cosine distance of each idea to the centroid (mean LaBSE embedding) of its condition (semantic divergence)
diversity_detail.computed_over: Each idea against the centroid of all ideas in its condition (AI-assisted or unaided), pooling both tasks and all participants
diversity_detail.uncertainty: Independent samples t-test over idea-level distances, treating ideas as independent; no adjustment for participant or task is reported; reported df 728 for 728 ideas
diversity_detail.notes: Direction conflict: the printed means (AI-assisted 0.29 vs unaided 0.28) and Fig. 3(a) show higher divergence for AI-assisted ideas, but the abstract and the text (pp. 1, 10, 13) say divergence was lower with AI. Each centroid pools the two task prompts in different proportions (AI-assisted: 195 Task 1 and 173 Task 2 ideas; unaided: 158 and 202; Fig. 1), so task mix also affects the distances.

eligibility.reason: Condition order was randomized: participants were assigned to ChatGPT (GPT-3.5) or unaided ideation for Task 1, then switched conditions for Task 2 (pp. 4-5, Section 3.2.1; p. 5, Fig. 1). The experiment reports 51 students and analyzes all 51, with 24 in Group A and 27 in Group B (p. 4, Section 3.1; p. 9, Table 5); no participant exclusions are reported. The analyzed sample is just above the 50-person threshold. Table 4 reports 51 per condition and N = 102 repeated person-condition observations, not 102 different people (p. 8). The first-period randomized comparison alone analyzes 27 AI-assisted and 24 unaided students with no prior experimental AI exposure. Creativity and diversity are scored on the submitted ideas, descriptions, and drawings, using category counts, word counts, drawing features, and semantic distances (pp. 5-7, Sections 3.2.2-3.3.2 and Table 2). Unresolved semantic-analysis details, scorer identity, and possible cross-paper sample reuse affect extraction or sample deduplication, not these eligibility criteria; the after-AI task/period limitation does not invalidate the first-period randomized comparison.

one_line_finding: Among 51 analyzed students, pooled within-person comparisons found more Existing Solutions with ChatGPT (1.00 vs 0.55, p = .011) and shorter descriptions (23.36 vs 25.57 words, p = .015), with no statistically significant differences in fluency, flexibility, or originality (p. 8, Table 4); thematic diversity was comparable (p. 10, Table 7 and Section 4.3), while semantic divergence was printed as higher with AI (0.29 vs 0.28) despite the narrative describing it as lower (p. 10, Section 4.3).
open_questions: Semantic divergence direction (S1-O7/S1-O8): means are printed as 0.28 unaided and 0.29 AI-assisted at both levels, and Fig. 3 shows higher divergence with AI, but the narrative says divergence was lower (pp. 1, 10-11, 13). Direction follows the printed means only; author clarification or the underlying data/code is needed to resolve the contradiction.

Semantic-test degrees of freedom and unit (S1-O7/S1-O8): the paper prints t(728) for the group-level test and t(364) for the individual-level paired test (p. 10, Section 4.3), while reporting 728 ideas and 51 analyzed students (pp. 5, 8-9). The actual independent units and handling of repeated observations require author clarification; no participant-level precision is inferred.

Individual semantic-divergence definition (S1-O7): Methods describe average pairwise divergence within each participant's own ideas (p. 7, Section 3.3.2), whereas Results and Fig. 3 describe divergence from the centroid per participant without identifying the centroid (pp. 10-11). Authors or their analysis code must identify the implemented measure.

After-AI task/period limitation (S1-O12 to S1-O15): the two unaided cells compare Group B in Task 2 after AI with Group A in Task 1 before AI, so task and period differ (p. 5, Section 3.2.1; p. 9, Table 5). The AI usage by condition order interaction uses both assisted and unaided scores (pp. 6, 8) and does not test that pair or isolate carryover. This is a documented design limitation; nothing further is needed for screening, and these records retain descriptive means only.

Image-elaboration scorer (S1-O6; also the unresolved reconciliation difference): Table 2 gives three yes/no drawing features, but no passage identifies who or what scored them (pp. 5-7, Sections 3.2.2-3.2.3 and Table 2). The measure code is null under the current spec; author clarification would settle the scorer.

Possible sample overlap with c201, Baltà-Salvador et al. (2025), Computer Applications in Engineering Education 33(1), e22817, DOI 10.1002/cae.22817: c031 cites this related work without saying whether the students are the same (p. 3, Section 1.1.4; p. 13, Section 5.3; p. 15, References). Author confirmation of participant identity is needed before treating the samples as independent.
Category-size level (S1-O10): Sections 3.3.2 and 4.3 (pp. 7, 10) do not identify whether the category-size comparison uses LV2 or LV3. Authors or their analysis code must identify the level.

Text-elaboration counting method (S1-O5): Table 2 specifies word count, but does not identify how it was counted (p. 7); the Gemini OCR description pertains to semantic analysis. The unsupported automated_score label is removed. Authors could clarify the counting method; a codebook convention would be needed to assign a measure code to a plain word count.
notes: Single study in one session at one university. All idea categorisation (flexibility, originality, novelty, thematic diversity) was done by the researchers on anonymised ideas without knowledge of the condition, settled by discussion to consensus, with no agreement statistic (p. 5). No human creativity ratings. Baseline balance: Groups A and B did not differ in five prior assignments or GPA (Table 3, p. 7; all p > .24). Ideas per cell: Group A Task 1 unaided 158, Group B Task 1 AI-assisted 195, Group B Task 2 unaided 202, Group A Task 2 AI-assisted 173 (Fig. 1, p. 5). Table 4 pools both tasks (N = 102 person-condition observations; Wilcoxon signed-rank); Table 5 gives Mann-Whitney tests by task. The Task 1 contrast is a between-person comparison with no prior exposure; the Task 2 contrasts are coded ai_vs_bau, but their control arm (Group B) had used ChatGPT in Task 1. Left out under the 15-outcome cap: after_ai versions of text elaboration (Group B Task 2 unaided 25.60 (7.39) vs Group A Task 1 unaided 25.54 (8.92)) and image elaboration (1.29 (0.36) vs 1.35 (0.35)), both in Table 5, p. 9. Not outcomes: prompt statistics (Table 8, 341 coded units in 49 conversations) and interaction codes (Table 9), p. 12. Data availability: 'Data will be made available on request.' (p. 15). Finalization: All 17 pages of the markdown were read through the end of References; the PDF has no appendix. Recorded outcome numbers were checked against PDF text, with Figures 1 and 3 also inspected. Separate omnibus ANOVA results (p. 6, Section 3.3.1; p. 8, Section 4.2): AI usage x condition order interaction for flexibility, Wilks’ lambda = 0.801, F(1, 49) = 12.19, p = .001, partial eta squared = 0.20; the corresponding originality interaction, Wilks’ lambda = 0.747, F(1, 49) = 16.62, p < .001, partial eta squared = 0.25; and the condition-order main effect for Existing Solutions, F(1, 49) = 1.56, p = .218, partial eta squared = 0.03. The paper reports no significant interactions for the remaining dimensions. These tests use both assisted and unaided observations and are not tests of the two unaided cells recorded as after_ai contrasts. Those contrasts retain arm descriptives only, with direction reflecting the printed means and the novelty sign reversal, not a significance or causal claim. Task 2 Mann-Whitney tests for flexibility and originality remain under S1-O2/S1-O3, where the tested arms match. Current-spec cleanup: unconfirmed measure codes in S1-O5 and S1-O6 are null; supplement existence is not_stated because none is referenced. The reconciliation object is preserved as historical review; the final corrections supersede its statements about measure codes and placement of ANOVA statistics.

open_items.item: S1-O7/S1-O8: semantic-divergence direction conflicts between printed means/Fig. 3 and narrative (pp. 10-11, 13); authors must correct the labels or interpretation, or supply the underlying data/code. This affects effect extraction, not eligibility.

S1-O7/S1-O8: semantic-test degrees of freedom and independent units are unclear (pp. 7, 10); authors must identify the actual analysis units and treatment of repeated observations. Other participant-level creativity outcomes establish eligibility.

S1-O7: pairwise-within-person versus centroid semantic-divergence definition conflicts (pp. 7, 10-11); authors or their analysis code must identify the implemented measure. This affects construct and precision coding, not eligibility.

S1-O12 to S1-O15: after-AI contrasts compare different tasks and periods and have no direct reported tests (pp. 5-6, 8-9). This limitation is settled from the reported design and retained in the form; no further material is needed for screening. The first-period randomized comparison remains eligible.

S1-O6 and the unresolved reconciliation difference: the image-elaboration scorer is unidentified (pp. 5-7). Authors must identify who or what scored the drawing rubric; measure is null. The outcome is clearly scored on drawings, so scorer identity does not affect criterion 3.

Possible shared participants with c201 / DOI 10.1002/cae.22817 (c031 pp. 3, 13, 15): authors must confirm participant overlap. This affects sample deduplication, not whether c031 analyzes at least 50 people or meets the other criteria.
S1-O10: the LV2 or LV3 level used for category size is unspecified (pp. 7, 10); authors or their analysis code must identify it. This affects measure detail, not output-based outcome eligibility.

S1-O5: the word-counting method is unspecified (p. 7, Table 2); authors could identify it. The unsupported measure code has been replaced with null; any codebook convention for plain word counts is a separate coding decision. Output-based eligibility is unaffected.
